opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, the virtual cell is one of my dream projects. I've been thinking about it for a long time, really since before AlphaFold. The way I see it, it's a hierarchy, and we're working our way up it step by step.

AlphaFold was the first rung: getting the static structure of individual proteins right. Then with the later versions we started looking at interactions, how proteins bind to other proteins, to DNA, RNA, small molecules, ligands. That matters because biology isn't really about single static structures. It's about dynamics and interactions, things coming together and coming apart. On the genetics side, there's work on predicting what a mutation actually does, whether a variant is likely to be benign or pathogenic, and on reading the regulatory code in the genome. Each of those is a building block.

The next step is to put the building blocks together into pathways, then into larger interacting systems, and eventually into a full simulation of a cell. I think a good first target is something like a yeast cell, a relatively simple and very well-studied organism that we have lots of data on. If you could model that well enough to run virtual experiments, perturb a gene, add a compound, and have the predictions match what you see in the wet lab, that would be extraordinarily powerful. You could do a huge amount of the search in silico, much faster and cheaper, and only use the lab to validate the most promising hypotheses.

The hard part is that you can't simulate a cell from first principles at the atomic level. It's computationally intractable, and it always will be at that scale. So the real question is what the right level of abstraction is. What can you coarse-grain away, and what details do you have to keep? That's where I think learned models come in. They can find efficient representations of these systems the way AlphaFold found a shortcut around brute-force physics simulation of folding.

The other bottleneck is data. For proteins we had the Protein Data Bank, decades of painstaking experimental work. For whole cells we need richer, more dynamic measurements, and I think a lot of progress will come from new kinds of experimental data generated specifically to train these models.

So I'd say we're maybe a few years away from something meaningful there. It's one of those things that seemed like pure science fiction ten years ago, and now I think it's a tractable research program. If we get there, it changes how we do biology and medicine. It moves us from biology as mostly an experimental science toward something closer to an engineering discipline.

r001.rationale: The response identifies predicting the effects of mutations and genetic variants as a building block, then places those building blocks on the path toward modeling pathways and a full cell.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that's one of the dreams I've had for a long time, actually, this idea of a virtual cell. If you look at the progression, we started with AlphaFold, which was about the static structure of a single protein. Then with AlphaFold 3 we moved to interactions, so proteins with DNA, RNA, ligands, small molecules, how these things actually bind to each other. And that's already a step up in complexity, because biology is really all about interactions. Nothing in the cell does anything on its own.

The next step is dynamics. Right now we're mostly predicting snapshots, and a cell is obviously not a snapshot, it's this incredibly busy, almost chaotic system with thousands of things happening at once, all of them influencing each other. So you need to model not just what the structures are, but how they move and change over time, how a pathway responds when you perturb it, what happens when you introduce a genetic mutation and it cascades through the whole system.

And I think the way to get there is to build it up layer by layer. You model the proteins, then the interactions, then maybe a single pathway, then a simple organism's cell, something like yeast, where we have a huge amount of data and we can actually test predictions in the lab. The key thing, as with AlphaFold, is having a tight loop between the model and experiment. You make predictions, you go and check them, and you use the errors to improve the model. That's what makes it scientific rather than just a simulation that looks plausible.

If we can do that, if we can have a virtual cell that's accurate enough to run experiments in silico, then I think it changes drug discovery, it changes how we understand disease, because you could test thousands of hypotheses before you ever touch a petri dish. I'd guess that's somewhere on the order of a decade of work, maybe less with the pace things are moving. But it's exactly the kind of problem where I think AI as a tool for science really shines. It's complex, it's high dimensional, there's lots of data, and humans just can't hold all of it in their heads at once.

r001.rationale: The response describes modeling what happens when a genetic mutation is introduced and how its effects cascade through the system, as part of the stepwise progression toward a virtual cell.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s one of the most exciting directions we can go in. If you think about proteins as the building blocks, understanding their structures is an important first step. But then you need to understand how they interact, how those interactions change over time, and how the cell regulates all of that.

The jump to a whole cell is enormous, because it isn’t just a bag of proteins. There’s spatial organization, there are feedback loops, and processes happening on very different timescales. So I suspect we’ll get there by modeling subsystems and then learning how to connect them, with experiments continually testing whether those models are actually predictive.

For me, a really useful milestone would be a virtual cell where you could ask: what happens if I change this gene, or introduce this molecule? And then reliably predict the consequences. You wouldn’t necessarily need to simulate every atom to do that. You’d need the right level of abstraction, and discovering what that is is part of the scientific challenge.

If we could achieve that, it would be an extraordinary tool for understanding disease and designing treatments. But there’s still a lot of work between predicting individual molecular properties and capturing the behavior of a living system.

r001.rationale: The response describes predicting consequences of changing a gene as a virtual-cell milestone, but does not say that predicting the functional effects of small genetic changes is an incremental step toward modeling an entire cell.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s one of the most exciting directions we can go in. If you think about what a cell is doing, proteins are interacting with other proteins, with DNA and RNA, with small molecules. Understanding the structures and interactions of those components gives you a foundation. But an entire cell is a dynamic system, so you also need to understand how those interactions change over time, how they’re regulated, and how the cell responds to its environment.

One way to approach that is to build models at different scales and then connect them. Can you predict what happens to a protein when you introduce a mutation? Then can you predict how that changes a pathway, and ultimately what happens to the cell? Each step gives you something you can test experimentally.

The ambition would be a virtual cell where you could ask, ‘What happens if I knock out this gene, or introduce this molecule?’ and get a useful prediction. That could be enormously powerful for understanding disease and discovering drugs. But there’s a big gap between knowing the parts and understanding the whole system. I think closing that gap will require a very tight loop between AI models and experiments.

r001.rationale: It describes predicting the effect of introducing a mutation on a protein, then tracing that change through a pathway to the cell, presenting these as connected steps toward a virtual cell model.
